input: This worked example looks at a vapour-compression refrigeration unit that serves a process chiller, evaporating at -25 °C and condensing at 35 °C, and it compares the performance that the unit actually achieves with the best performance that could possibly be achieved between the same two temperatures. The best possible performance is given by the Carnot coefficient of performance, 4.13 in this case, and in order to calculate it the temperatures must first of all be converted to the absolute scale. Adding 273 to each temperature gives 248 K for the evaporating temperature and 308 K for the condensing temperature, a difference of 60 K between them. The Carnot coefficient of performance is the evaporating temperature divided by this difference, so it comes to 248 divided by 60, which is 4.13. The installed unit, by comparison, achieves a coefficient of performance of only 1.8, a figure that is taken from the manufacturer's test carried out at full load. It can be seen that the achieved value of 1.8 lies well below the Carnot value of 4.13, as it must do, since no real machine can exceed the Carnot limit. Finally, it should be noted that the manufacturer's figure relates to full-load operation only, and the performance of the unit at part load is not stated, so nothing can be said about how the unit performs away from the full-load condition. It is the 1.8 from the manufacturer's test, and not the ideal figure, that a designer would carry into an estimate of the chiller duty, and the shortfall of the 1.8 below the ideal value is the margin absorbed by the losses of the real machine.
target: A vapour-compression unit serving a process chiller evaporates at -25 °C and condenses at 35 °C. Between those two temperatures the Carnot coefficient of performance (COP) is 4.13, and the installed unit achieves 1.8. The coefficient of performance states the duty obtained for the work supplied: the heat removed at the evaporating side, divided by the work the compressor takes in. A higher figure means more cooling bought with the same work, and the measure allows machines of different sizes to be compared on equal terms, because both the duty and the work scale with the size of the unit while their ratio does not. The Carnot figure is calculated on the absolute scale. Adding 273 to each temperature gives an evaporating temperature of 248 K and a condensing temperature of 308 K, a difference of 60 K. The Carnot COP is the evaporating temperature divided by the difference between the two temperatures: 248 divided by 60, which is 4.13. No machine working between the same temperatures can exceed that value. The achieved COP of 1.8 comes from the manufacturer's test at full load. Set against the Carnot value, the comparison checks the result before it is used: 1.8 lies below 4.13, as the second law requires, and the gap between the two values is the performance the real cycle loses to the irreversibilities the Carnot cycle does not have. The scope of the achieved figure is narrow. Part-load performance is not stated, and the manufacturer's test says nothing about operation away from full load. The 1.8 is a full-load value for the stated evaporating and condensing temperatures; a duty at other temperatures, or at part load, needs its own figure and does not inherit this one. For the chiller duty the figure to carry forward is the achieved one, with its full-load condition attached to it. The Carnot value serves as the reference the achieved figure is judged against, and the two values are not interchangeable in a duty calculation.
